nameStory: The band-winged meadowhawk gets its name from the distinctive dark bands that streak across its wings, making it easy to spot among its meadowhawk cousins. Like other meadowhawks, it's often found in grassy areas near water where it hunts for insects. The 'hawk' part of the name comes from these dragonflies' fierce hunting style - they're aerial predators that snatch mosquitoes and flies right out of the air.
description: The band-winged meadowhawk is a medium-sized dragonfly that belongs to the skimmer family, one of New England's most common dragonfly groups. These agile hunters have sturdy bodies that turn red in mature males, while females stay more yellowish-brown. They're about 1.5 inches long with a wingspan around 2.5 inches. You'll often see them perching on low plants or fence posts, then darting out to catch flying insects before returning to the same spot.

idTips.label: Wing bands
idTips.description: Look for dark amber or brownish bands across the middle of each wing - these bands are most visible when the dragonfly is at rest and you can see the wings spread out

idTips.label: Male coloring
idTips.description: Mature males have bright red bodies that feel warm to the touch in sunlight, with the red color most intense on the abdomen

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: They return repeatedly to the same favorite perch, often a sturdy plant stem or low post that feels secure under their weight

idTips.label: Wing position
idTips.description: At rest, wings are held horizontally out from the body rather than folded back - if you approach slowly, you can see the transparent wing membranes with their dark bands

idTips.label: Female appearance
idTips.description: Females have yellowish-brown bodies with darker markings and the same distinctive wing bands, but their colors are more muted than males

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Strong, direct fliers that make audible wing beats - you can often hear them approaching before you see them

habitat: Band-winged meadowhawks prefer open areas near still or slow-moving water like ponds, marshes, and quiet stream backwaters throughout New England. You'll find them in sunny meadows, old fields, and wetland edges where they can easily spot prey from their perches. They're especially common around cattail marshes and in areas where grasses meet water.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with newly emerged individuals having pale, soft bodies that haven't yet developed their full coloring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in mid to late summer when fully mature adults are most colorful and active, with males establishing territories near water.
seasonality.fall: Still active into early fall, often one of the last dragonfly species you'll see before frost, with some individuals flying into October during warm spells.
seasonality.winter: Not active - adults die with the first hard frost, while eggs overwinter in pond sediments and shallow water.

funFact: Band-winged meadowhawks can actually change their body temperature by adjusting their posture - on cool mornings, they'll angle their bodies perpendicular to the sun's rays to absorb maximum heat, but on hot afternoons, they'll point their abdomens directly at the sun to minimize heating and avoid overheating.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other meadowhawk species, but the wing bands are your best clue - no other New England meadowhawk has such obvious dark bands across the wings. Remember: 'bands on wings, you've found the right thing!'
contextualKnowledge: The meadowhawk group can be tricky for beginners because there are seven species in New England, and females of different species often look very similar. Wing patterns and male coloration are usually your best identification features, but don't worry if it takes practice to tell them apart reliably.
compareHints: Among New England meadowhawks, the band-winged is the only one with prominent dark wing bands - ruby meadowhawks have clear wings and bright red males, while autumn meadowhawks lack wing bands and have more orange-red coloring. White-faced meadowhawks have distinctive white faces, making the band-winged meadowhawk's wing markings the easiest field mark to spot.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, Autumn Meadowhawks are distinguished by their completely yellow legs - most other meadowhawks have black legs or black stripes on their legs.
Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, the white-faced is the only one where males develop a pure white face - other meadowhawks have reddish, yellowish, or dark faces.

Among New England's meadowhawks, the Saffron-winged is most easily distinguished by its golden wing stripes in younger individuals and females, while the Ruby Meadowhawk typically shows clearer wings and the White-faced has a distinctly pale face.

Cherry-faced meadowhawks are distinguished from other meadowhawks primarily by their very dark red, almost burgundy faces when mature, compared to the brighter reds of ruby meadowhawks or the white faces of white-faced meadowhawks.
